help.label: About sounds
help.text:
An agent in any project calls you with a sound: when it finishes, asks for something, hits a limit or breaks. Its chat tab glows in the colour of the reason, and the project tab gets a dot of the same colour, until you open that chat.

A muted sound doesn't call at all: no glow and no dot. While you look right at a chat, it stays quiet. Of sounds that come at once, only the more important one plays.

google.agentFailed: {{app}} didn't open. Copy the prompt and paste it there.
google.agentPrompt:
Set up a Google OAuth client for Agentic Workstation, a desktop app, in my Google account, working in my browser. I'm already signed in to Google. If a site asks for a sign-in, a 2-step code, a payment method or accepting terms, stop and ask me.

The goal: any Google account I choose can sign in to Gmail and Calendar in Agentic Workstation. For that the app has to be published ("In production"). Google publishes only apps with a home page and a privacy policy on a domain I own and have verified in Google Search Console. Free shared addresses (github.io, web.app, blogspot.com, Google Sites) don't count.

1. Open https://console.cloud.google.com/ and create a new project named "Agentic Workstation". If a project with this name already exists, use it. Don't change any other project.
2. In that project, open APIs & Services > Library and enable "Gmail API" and "Google Calendar API".
3. Open Google Auth Platform (https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/overview). If it asks to get started: app name "Agentic Workstation", user support email and developer contact email - my email, audience - External. Don't add scopes under Data Access: the app asks for them at sign-in.
4. In Google Auth Platform > Clients, create a client: application type "Desktop app", name "Agentic Workstation". Download its JSON file right in the dialog that appears after creating it: Google shows the client secret only once. If the dialog closed without the download, create one more client the same way. The file is named like client_secret_....json and goes to Downloads. Tell me its name: I can already choose it in the IDE.
5. Ask me whether I have my own domain and where its DNS is managed. Don't guess it.
If I have one:
a. Put two public pages on it: a home page and a privacy policy, on the same domain (for example https://example.com/agentic-workstation and https://example.com/agentic-workstation/privacy, or a subdomain). Use the hosting I already have for this domain. If I have none, offer a free hosting that serves my own domain (Cloudflare Pages, GitHub Pages) and ask before creating accounts or projects there.
The home page: Agentic Workstation is a desktop IDE for macOS and Windows; it connects my own Gmail and Google Calendar to the AI assistants inside the IDE, so they can search and read mail, manage drafts and labels, and read and change calendar events; sending mail and invitations stays off until I turn it on. Link to the privacy policy from it.
The privacy policy: the app reads and changes Gmail messages, drafts and labels and Calendar events and calendars only to do what I ask in the IDE; sign-in tokens are stored encrypted on my computer and never sent to the app developer; mail and events the AI reads are sent to the AI provider I use in the IDE (for example Anthropic for Claude) as part of the conversation; the data is not sold or used for advertising; access can be revoked at https://myaccount.google.com/permissions; a contact email - mine. Add this sentence: "Agentic Workstation's use and transfer of information received from Google APIs adheres to the Google API Services User Data Policy, including the Limited Use requirements."
b. Verify the domain in Google Search Console (https://search.google.com/search-console) with this same Google account: a Domain property, confirmed by a DNS TXT record. Only add new DNS records, never change or delete existing ones, and ask me before adding.
c. In Google Auth Platform > Branding, fill in the app home page and privacy policy links and add the domain under Authorized domains. Don't upload a logo: it needs a separate review by Google. Save.
d. In Google Auth Platform > Audience, press "Publish app" and confirm. If Google says the app needs verification, skip it: the app is for my own use.
If I have no domain, or "Publish app" stays unavailable, tell me why and offer two ways: buy a domain and continue from step a, or leave the app in "Testing" and add the Google accounts I name under Audience > Test users. In testing mode only test users can sign in, and Google asks them to sign in again every 7 days.

Don't copy the client secret anywhere and don't paste it into any chat or form. At the end, tell me whether the app is published or which test users you added.

description.title: Description
description.placeholder: What it is and when to use it

page.title: About connectors
page.text:
Connectors belong to the IDE, not to an AI account. Every AI panel sees them, and switching the Claude account keeps them signed in.

Add as many of one kind as you need: work and personal mail side by side.

Each connector chooses its projects: all of them or only the ones you pick. Open a connector to change its sign-in, projects and tools.

description.title: Description
description.text:
Your own words about this connector: what it is and when to use it.

The AI gets the description together with the connector, so it can tell similar connectors apart and pick the right one - say, which Playwright server is for which project.

It saves as you type.

projects.title: Projects
projects.text:
All projects: every project sees the connector, new ones too.

Selected only: only the projects switched on see it. New projects don't get it.

Switching to Selected only starts with every project on, so nothing changes until you switch some off.

tools.title: Tools
tools.text:
Tools are grouped by what they do: Read only looks, Write changes your own data, Sends to people sends messages, emails or posts that other people see.

Sending tools are off by default. Only you can turn them on here; the AI can't.

The refresh button asks the service for its tools again.

forgotten.title: Other folders
forgotten.text: Settings kept for folders that aren't among open or recent projects - renamed, moved or long closed. Move them to the folder's new project, or forget the ones that are gone.

add.name: The label tells connections of one connector apart: Work, Personal. Latin letters and digits.
add.custom:
Name: how the connector is called everywhere, with a capital letter - Playwright, Linear. Server names come from it once and don't change when you rename it: rules and hooks rely on them.

Several connections: connect it more than once, like Gmail. Each connection gets its own label and sign-in. Such a connector shows up in Apps, marked Custom, and you can remove it from there.
add.gmail: Gmail signs in through your own Google app: set it up once above, then add as many accounts as you need. You sign in in your browser.
add.calendar: Google Calendar signs in through your own Google app: set it up once above, then add as many accounts as you need. You sign in in your browser.
add.notion: Notion connects through its official MCP server. You sign in in your browser and pick the workspace there.
add.slack:
Slack lets only apps made inside a workspace, or published in the Slack Marketplace, use its MCP. So each workspace gets its own small Slack app, and each app gets its own connector: add another connector for another workspace.

Create Slack app opens Slack with the app ready: the redirect URL and the permissions the Slack MCP asks for are filled in. Model Context Protocol is the one switch Slack doesn't let set in advance.

If the workspace needs an admin to approve apps, Slack asks the admin first.

Using an app you already have? Add http://localhost:5319/callback as a redirect URL under OAuth & Permissions.
add.atlassian:
Jira and Confluence on Atlassian Cloud - sites like yourteam.atlassian.net - through Atlassian's official MCP server. You sign in in your browser and allow access to your sites there.

Jira and Confluence on a company's own server (Data Center) don't work through it.
add.todoist:
Todoist through its official MCP server, signed in with your API token: Todoist → Settings → Integrations → Developer → API token.

The token doesn't expire. If you reset it in Todoist, replace it in the connector.
add.playwright:
A browser the AI drives through the Playwright MCP server on this computer. Each conversation starts its own copy of it, like in Claude Code.

Clean each time: the browser forgets everything between runs. Saved: it keeps cookies and sign-ins in its folder, so the AI stays signed in to sites. A saved profile works in one conversation at a time.

Version: latest by default. Pin a number if latest breaks your saved profile.
add.mcp:
Any remote MCP server by its address.

Browser: the server asks you to sign in. Token: sent with every request as Authorization: Bearer. None: an open server, or one on this computer.
add.command:
An MCP server this computer starts: npx, node or a script. Each conversation starts its own copy, like in Claude Code.

Environment variables are kept encrypted in the IDE, not in any config file. The command runs from your home folder with your shell PATH.
add.http:
Describe a service: the AI reads its API docs and builds the connector as a list of HTTP requests, not code. It takes a few minutes, and you can close this window meanwhile: the result waits in the catalog.

Check what the AI built before adding it. Your API key is stored encrypted in the IDE; the AI that built the connector never sees it.
add.import: Your MCP servers from Claude Code settings become connectors with the same names. Keys move into the IDE vault; Claude Code settings stay as they are.
add.browser:
The AI works in your real Chrome, with your sign-ins: it opens tabs in its own orange tab group in the background, or takes a tab you share with Copy tab reference for AI (right-click on a page). While it works you see an orange frame and its cursor; your current tab and focus stay yours.

Add the connector, then install the extension in Chrome once - the steps are in the connector window. Each Chrome profile with the extension connects on its own.

type.title: Custom connector
type.text:
A connector you added yourself. Each connection gets its own label and sign-in; the command or the address is shared.

Removing the connector removes its connections too.

google.title: Google sign-in
google.text:
Google has no shared sign-in app for desktop IDEs, so Gmail and Calendar sign in through your own Google app. You create it once, and it serves every Gmail and Calendar connector.

The JSON file is that app's ID card: Google gives it to you when you create an OAuth client. It holds the app's ID and secret, not your password or mail. The IDE keeps it encrypted and uses it only to open Google's sign-in page.

Set up with AI opens Claude or Codex with the setup prompt ready. Send it there: the AI clicks through Google Cloud Console in your browser and downloads the file, then you choose it here. For another AI, copy the prompt.

To let any of your Google accounts sign in, the app has to be published, and Google publishes only apps with a home page and privacy policy on a domain you own. The AI makes the pages and verifies the domain with you. Without a domain the app stays in testing: only accounts added as test users can sign in, and Google asks them to sign in again every 7 days.

When you sign in, Google warns that the app isn't verified. It's your own app: continue.

browser.title: Browser for the AI
browser.text:
The extension connects Chrome to Agentic Workstation through a small helper that Chrome starts itself; nothing listens on a network port.

Each conversation gets its own orange tab group. When the AI finishes, it closes its tabs and the group, and lets go of the tabs you shared. Stop in the extension window ends it at any time; so does Cancel on Chrome's "started debugging" bar.

Copy tab reference for AI (right-click on a page or on the extension icon) copies a reference the AI understands: paste it into the chat to point it at that tab. A reference works until Chrome restarts. The AI tells profiles apart by the name you give each one in the extension window.

The AI can see and use every tab of a connected profile. Uploading files to a site is off until you turn it on in the connector's tools, and even then the AI uploads and opens only files inside the conversation's project. Turn the connector off or limit it to some projects to keep it out.

help.label: About local history
help.title: Local history
help.text:
Every change to the project's files is kept for {{days}} days: saves in the editor, edits by AI agents and other programs, renames, moves and deletions. Files that git ignores are kept too once you open them in the editor or an agent edits them.

With Current puts the selected version on the left and the file as it is now on the right. The right side is the file itself: edit it, or bring back a single change with the arrow between the sides. This Change shows what the selected event did to the file.

Restore puts the whole version back into the file, and brings a deleted file back. Nothing is lost: what was in the file before stays in local history as its own version.

scenarios.title: Scenarios
scenarios.noProject: Open a project to see its scenarios and queues.

help.label: About scenarios
help.title: Scenarios
help.text:
A scenario is a round of work written once: stages with cards that an AI agent goes through, while a main thread reads each result and decides what comes next.

You run scenarios in queues. A queue is a line of work with its own name: scenarios in it run one after another, and each one sees what the previous ones did. Queues run side by side, so start a new one for unrelated work.

A queue can work in the project folder or in its own git worktree - a separate copy of the repository on its own branch, so parallel queues do not touch each other or your files. The worktree stays after the queue ends, until you remove it.

Pause stops the running scenario at once and keeps everything in memory. Stop after current lets it finish and starts nothing after it. Stop after a chosen scenario lets the queue run up to it.

A scenario on this shelf is a file in the project's .claude/scenarios folder. It travels with the repository: everyone working here has it, next to the project's own commands and skills.

Drag a scenario by its handle to change the order or to move it onto the other shelf - its file moves with it. With the handle focused, {{up}} and {{down}} do the same.

Drag a scenario by its handle to change the order or to move it onto the other shelf - its file moves with it. With the handle focused, {{up}} and {{down}} do the same.

help.label: About this run
help.title: A run
help.text:
A run is one pass of a scenario. Cards do the work, each in its own conversation, and the main thread reads what every card did and decides what comes next: send it back, move on or stop.

Log on a card opens that card's conversation as it is. Main thread opens the main thread's own conversation: how it read each card and why it decided what it did.

Write to the main thread at the bottom. It reads your words between cards and answers in the timeline.

Pause keeps everything alive and goes on from the same place. Stop cuts the current card short. A stopped or failed run can be continued: the same main thread picks up where it stood.

help.label: How a scenario works
help.title: Scenario editor
help.text:
A scenario is stages with cards. Each card is a job for its own AI session; the main thread reads what the card did, judges it by your briefing and decides what comes next.

A prompt writes {{name}} where an answer to a question asked before the run goes, and [[name]] where the main thread fills in what the cards above found out. Both are lit up as you type.

Problems are listed under the outline: red ones keep the scenario from running, yellow ones are worth tidying. Choosing the other shelf moves the file when you save.

page.title: Statistics
page.text:
What your agents and you did over the chosen period. Agent numbers cover the whole computer: every Claude Code session on it, read from its transcripts. Claude Code keeps them for about 30 days, so older history is whatever is still on disk. Your own numbers, presence and code by hand, are counted only in this IDE window and only from the day statistics appeared.

Today is the current day; 7 days and 30 days end today. Each number is compared with the same stretch of the previous period up to the same point: today is compared with yesterday by this time. There is no comparison when the previous period starts before the data does.

In IDE means conversations in the Claude Code panel and scenario runs started by this IDE. Outside IDE is everything else, such as Claude Code in a terminal. Your presence and code by hand are always yours and do not depend on this filter. This project keeps only work in the folder of the project that is open now.

overview.title: Overview
overview.text:
Code: lines added and removed, by you in the IDE editor and by agents through successful file edits. The bar shows whose lines they are.

Agent time: how long agent turns ran, added up, so two agents working for an hour make two hours. Wall-clock is the time when at least one agent was working. Part of the time outside the IDE is an estimate from transcripts, and the bar shows how much.

Your presence: minutes when the IDE window was focused and you typed, clicked or scrolled within the last 3 minutes.

Tokens and cost: everything the models read and wrote. Cost is at public API prices, not what a subscription charges you.

code.title: Code
code.text:
Code by hand is what you typed in the IDE editor. Each save is compared with the previous save, and only your own changes count: files reloaded from disk, undo and redo do not. Typed and pasted characters are counted separately.

Code by agents comes from successful file edits in Claude Code transcripts, including edits made with shell commands. Failed edits do not count. Each file is counted once. Languages are grouped by file extension.

time.title: Time
time.text:
Agent turns, summed: each turn from your message to the agent's last step. Turns that run at the same time add up. In the IDE this is measured live, without the time an agent waits for your answer. Outside the IDE it is an estimate from transcripts: a turn ends at its last entry, and gaps longer than 15 minutes are not counted.

Wall-clock: time when at least one agent was working. Agents worked without you: wall-clock time outside your presence minutes.

Your presence: a minute counts when the IDE window was focused and you used the keyboard, mouse or scroll within the last 3 minutes.

habits.title: When you work
habits.text:
The calendar always covers the last year, whatever the period above. Each square is a day: the brighter it is, the busier the day compared with your other active days. A day is active when you were present in the IDE or sent a message to an agent. The current streak does not break until today is over.

The busiest days and hours are three days in a row and three hours in a row with the most presence, or with the most tokens while there is no presence yet. A work session is a stretch of presence; a break longer than 30 minutes starts a new one.

tokens.title: Tokens & cost
tokens.text:
Tokens from every answer of every model, subagents included, each counted once. Cost is calculated at public API prices for each model, with cache reads and writes at their own rates. It is not what a subscription charges you.

Cache read is the part of the model input that came from the prompt cache: the larger it is, the cheaper long conversations get. A session belongs to the project of the folder it ran in; Other folders are those outside any project the IDE knows.

scenarios.title: Scenarios
scenarios.text: Scenario runs that started in the period. Finished successfully is the share of done runs among runs that ended: done, failed or stopped by you. Active time is the time the agent actually worked, without waiting for you. Scenarios run only in the IDE, so Outside IDE never has any.

tools.title: Tools
tools.text: Tool calls by agents, from transcripts. Connector tools (MCP) are grouped by their server. Permission questions are the ones you answered in the IDE panel: how many were asked, allowed and denied.

accounts.help:
Chats run on the account in use. Each account keeps only its own sign-in: chats, settings, skills, hooks, plugins and history are shared.

Add account opens a Terminal window for the sign-in. Your existing account is not touched.

Connectors (Gmail, Notion, Slack and MCP servers) belong to the IDE, not to the account: switching keeps them signed in.

Claude Design signs in per account too, and only a terminal can do it. Authorize Claude Design opens one for the account in use; DesignSync then works in the panel by itself.

help.label: What the phone can do
help.title: What the phone can do
help.text:
The phone sees open and recent projects, the conversations of each provider (Claude Code now), the scenario queues, the provider accounts and the IDE connectors. The phone knows a project by a key, not by its folder: in what it reads, the project, worktree and home folders are shortened to {project}, {worktree} and ~. Email addresses reach it masked.

In a conversation the phone can read the feed, write a message with photos or queue it while a turn runs, reorder, remove or send a queued message now, answer a permission request, a question or a plan, dismiss a question, stop the turn or force-stop its process, stop a background agent, say Don't continue after a usage limit, ask a side question, rewind to a message, search past conversations, start a new conversation, rename it and change its model, effort or fast mode.

In scenarios the phone can read a scenario in full, duplicate or delete it, let AI draft a new one, schedule runs, start a scenario in a new or existing queue, pause, resume and stop a run, answer its head, write to it, read a step's log, continue after a limit, star or delete past runs, and remove, move, rename, clear or stop a queue after an item.

On this computer the phone can open a recent project, see account usage, switch, rename, forget or sign out of an account, and reconnect a connector.

The phone cannot use the terminal or ! commands, edit files, install plugins, change IDE or provider settings, add accounts or sign in, add, remove or sign in to connectors, pair other phones, allow a tool "always", turn on bypass or auto mode, close a queue or delete worktrees.

Everything travels end-to-end encrypted through your own relay, which only routes frames by address and cannot read them. The relay also serves the phone app, so the phone trusts that server to send the genuine app. Revoke a phone here and its key stops working at once.
